reason: This passage (Nehemiah 5) depicts Nehemiah, acting as God's appointed governor, taking decisive action to relieve the Hebrew people's economic suffering and oppression. He explicitly frames his opposition to exploitation through the lens of 'fear of God' (יִרְאַת אֱלֹהִים), implying that God's will is offended by the oppression of His people. Nehemiah forbears from collecting taxes that would burden them further, restores their mortgaged property, and cancels debts—all positioned as righteous actions worthy of God's remembrance. The relief of the people's suffering is presented not as Nehemiah's arbitrary preference but as alignment with God's standards for justice and treatment of the covenant people. The text's framing of these acts as morally binding under appeal to God demonstrates an implicit theological claim that God cares about the wellbeing of the Hebrew people.
